faq: What does this tool calculate?
The spherical mean (centre of direction) of a set of coordinate pairs — the point minimising the group's angular spread, computed via 3D vector averaging.
Which map standard does it use?
WGS84 coordinates on a spherical Earth model — the standard for centre-finding at every scale this tool serves.
Can I use this in production GIS?
As the centroid method, yes — it matches what GIS spherical centroids compute. Ellipsoid-exact centroids for legal work remain the surveyor's domain.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84 throughout.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
The mean's honest precision is bounded by the inputs' spread and accuracy — extra decimals are arithmetic, and the tool's output should be read with the cluster's size in mind.
Weighted points?
Repeat a point to weight it — duplication is the transparent weighting mechanism, visible in the input itself.
Outliers drag the mean.
They do — that is a mean being a mean. For a resistant centre, trim the outliers or use the median-style point; the distances table shows each point's pull.
Mean of two points equals the midpoint?
Yes — the spherical mean of a pair is their great-circle midpoint, the halfway tools' foundation.
Antipodal points?
Points exactly opposite cancel — the mean is undefined, and the tool says so rather than inventing a centre.
Can I mean elevations too?
This tool means positions on the sphere. Elevation averages are a separate, simpler statistic.
Input formats?
Decimal pairs, one per line — dressed formats convert first in the Coordinate Converter.
